lifecycle.description: OKX opened X Layer public mainnet as a Polygon-CDK, ZK-powered EVM L2 integrated with its exchange and wallet.
X Layer completed its PP upgrade to the then-current Polygon CDK, targeting 5,000 TPS and negligible gas.
OKB minting and manual-burning functionality was removed after a one-time burn fixed supply at 21M.
The status log records a mainnet hard fork and op-geth end-of-support transition.

token.launch_relation: OKB predates X Layer; it became X Layer's sole native gas token and was migrated toward a fixed 21M-supply chain-native model in August 2025.

capital.notes: OKX launched and integrated X Layer. No standalone network financing total or current ecosystem-fund amount is asserted from reviewed primary sources.

onchain.methodology_note: Stablecoin supply is not TVL. The as-of TVL is also the observed history-series peak, so no decline is inferred.

team.entity: OKX launched and operates key X Layer integrations; Polygon technology underpins the CDK stack.

key_events.description: OKX launched X Layer with exchange and wallet distribution.
OKX and Polygon-stack changes drove the PP upgrade and new DeFi, payments, and RWA focus.

narrative.purpose: Connect OKX exchange, wallet, and payment distribution to low-cost ZK-EVM execution for DeFi, payments, and real-world assets.
narrative.positioning: An exchange-distributed Polygon-CDK L2 with OKB as fixed-supply gas and deep stablecoin float.
narrative.narrative_arc: X Layer moved from a broad OKX zkEVM to a payments, RWA, and DeFi-focused chain while consolidating OKTChain utility and OKB supply onto X Layer.

sanctions.detail: No chain-level designation is asserted; an archived exact-name SDN review remains an explicit gap.

risks.detail: Exchange, wallet, Pay, withdrawal, and token-migration distribution are tightly coupled to OKX systems and policy.
Frequent client, hard-fork, and Polygon-stack transitions create coordination and compatibility risk.
The OKB burn fixed supply but did not establish holder, governance, or sequencer-control dispersion in reviewed materials.

synthesis.situation: X Layer reports a new TVL high of $107.0M, $1.08B in 30-day DEX volume, and nearly $2.0B stablecoin supply while direct chain revenue remains small.
synthesis.why: X Layer gained activity because OKX could route exchange, wallet, stablecoin, and payment users into a low-cost compatible chain, then consolidated OKB and retired overlapping OKTChain utility.
synthesis.success_mechanism: Corporate distribution and stablecoin rails create transactions; the CDK supplies EVM compatibility and proofs; fixed-supply OKB captures gas demand.
strategic_choices: Use Polygon CDK rather than invent a proprietary VM.
Make OKB the sole gas and native token and retire overlapping OKTChain.
Refocus the chain on DeFi, payments, and RWAs with direct OKX product integration.
unknowns: Current sequencer, prover, upgrade-key, bridge, and application-TVL concentration.
How much stablecoin float and DEX volume is organic versus routed through OKX incentives.
Whether OKB gas demand produces material value capture when fees are intentionally negligible.
lessons_learned: Exchange distribution can create rapid liquidity and routing advantages.
Token consolidation simplifies identity but increases dependence on one corporate ecosystem.
High stablecoin supply and volume do not imply proportionate chain revenue.
synthesis.could_differ: Keeping OKTChain and Ethereum OKB in parallel would preserve optionality but fragment liquidity, identity, and maintenance.

outlook.bull: OKX Pay and exchange routing make X Layer a major settlement venue.
outlook.base: X Layer remains active and corporate-dependent with thin fee capture.
outlook.bear: Activity follows incentives or OKX policy elsewhere and stack upgrades create instability.

merger.title: GnosisDAO and Gnosis Chain merger history

stables.title: DefiLlama stablecoin supply by chain API

lifecycle.description: The xDai execution chain began operating with stablecoin-denominated gas.
xDai and Gnosis communities approved their merger into Gnosis Chain.
Gnosis execution merged with its Beacon Chain, replacing delegated proof-of-stake/POSDAO with permissionless proof of stake.
Canonical-bridge outflows were unfrozen after a precautionary halt related to the Gnosis Pay Delay Module hack.

token.launch_relation: GNO predates Gnosis Chain and secures proof-of-stake validators and DAO governance; xDAI, backed through the DAI bridge model, pays execution gas.

capital.historical_treasury_disclosure: Gnosis reported a large ETH/GNO treasury and launched a $40M GnosisVC fund, but this dossier does not mark those assets to the as-of date.
capital.notes: Historic token-auction proceeds and current DAO treasury require a reconciled primary ledger analysis before asserting a financing or treasury total.

onchain.methodology_note: The xDAI gas asset, bridged stablecoins, tracked DeFi TVL, and stablecoin circulating supply are distinct accounting categories.

founders.name: Martin Köppelmann
founders.prior: prediction markets and Ethereum ecosystem development

team.entity: GnosisDAO governs the ecosystem and treasury; Gnosis Chain is operated by a permissionless validator set, with separate bridge-governor and bridge-validator groups.

key_events.description: Gnosis began as an Ethereum prediction-market project.
GnosisDAO launched and assumed strategic governance.
The xDai/Gnosis merger created the present chain identity.

narrative.purpose: Provide credibly neutral, low-cost EVM execution with stable xDAI gas and a large home-staker validator set for open-finance and payment applications.
narrative.positioning: An Ethereum-like proof-of-stake sidechain differentiated by stable gas, DAO ownership, payments, Safe/CoW roots, and home staking.
narrative.narrative_arc: Gnosis evolved from prediction markets into Ethereum infrastructure, merged with xDai, and centered a user-owned open-finance stack around stable gas and broad validation.

exploits.detail: A Gnosis Pay Delay Module hack prompted precautionary canonical-bridge outflow freezes; this is not labeled a consensus exploit.
Compromised CoW and Hopr operational keys required canonical-bridge validator rotation.

sanctions.detail: No chain-level designation is asserted; an archived exact-name SDN review remains an explicit gap.

risk.audit_status: Canonical bridges advertise audits and a bug bounty, but a complete current chain-wide audit inventory is not reconciled.

risks.detail: Canonical xDAI and OmniBridge operations retain governor and validator threshold trust assumptions.
Multiple 2026 validator-key rotations show that independent operators can introduce bridge risk even without consensus failure.
GNO secures consensus while xDAI pays gas, so execution demand does not directly create GNO-denominated fee demand.

synthesis.situation: Gnosis retains $100.0M TVL and $159.2M in 30-day DEX volume, with TVL 65.7% below peak; 2026 bridge-key incidents required active governance response.
synthesis.postmortem: Recent bridge controls contained ecosystem and operator-key exposure, but demonstrate that the canonical bridge remains a separate trusted system despite permissionless chain consensus.
synthesis.why: Gnosis endures because stable gas, home-staker validation, DAO capital, and deeply used Ethereum infrastructure products give it a coherent open-finance niche beyond raw blockspace.
synthesis.success_mechanism: xDAI lowers payment friction; GNO staking secures consensus; GnosisDAO, Safe, CoW, and payment products provide applications and distribution.
strategic_choices: Merge xDai execution with GNO-secured beacon consensus.
Keep xDAI as stable gas while using GNO for staking and governance.
Prioritize community validation and open-finance products over general L1 marketing.
unknowns: Current validator-client, home-staker, bridge-signer, and application-TVL concentration.
A reconciled current GnosisDAO treasury and chain-development spending history.
Whether Hashi or other trust-minimized bridge upgrades materially reduce multisig dependence.
lessons_learned: Permissionless consensus does not make canonical bridges trustless.
Stable gas improves UX but separates transaction demand from staking-token demand.
Operational-key rotation and bridge freezes are important lifecycle evidence, not footnotes.
synthesis.could_differ: Using GNO for gas would tighten value capture but sacrifice the predictable stable-fee experience.

outlook.bull: Gnosis payments and open-finance products convert stable gas and home staking into durable growth.
outlook.base: Gnosis remains resilient and useful, with bridge trust and modest liquidity.
outlook.bear: Bridge or governance failures erode confidence faster than app adoption grows.

stables.title: DefiLlama stablecoin supply by chain API

lifecycle.description: Stellar and the nonprofit Stellar Development Foundation launched with Jed McCaleb and Joyce Kim.
The present Stellar public network launched under the Stellar Consensus Protocol; its passphrase records September 2015.
Validator quorum configuration caused a 67-minute network halt without fork or fund loss.
Soroban became user-ready on mainnet after the Protocol 20 phased rollout.
A Protocol 23 archival bug was found after corrupting 478 entries; 84 required downstream mitigations after repair.

token.launch_relation: The present-network lumens launched with the 2015 SCP network; 100B original supply was later reduced through burns and inflation was disabled.

capital.notes: SDF's XLM mandate and $100M Soroban adoption commitment are ecosystem resources, not reconciled venture financing or a marked-to-market treasury.

onchain.methodology_note: Stellar's payment and asset-issuance activity is broader than DeFi TVL and tracked spot DEX volume; stablecoin supply is reported separately.

founders.name: David Mazières
founders.prior: Stanford computer-science professor and security researcher

team.entity: Stellar Development Foundation is a US nonprofit supporting open-source development and ecosystem growth; independent validators select quorums and approve upgrades.

key_events.description: David Mazières published SCP and the network relaunched on it.

team.regulatory_status: SDF is a US nonprofit; this is organizational status, not a regulatory classification of XLM.

narrative.purpose: Connect financial institutions and users through fast asset issuance, payments, foreign-exchange paths, and Soroban smart contracts.
narrative.positioning: A payments-first L1 with native asset primitives, federated Byzantine consensus, institutional rails, and a newer WASM smart-contract layer.
narrative.narrative_arc: Stellar spent a decade optimizing payments and asset issuance, then added Soroban to broaden into programmable finance without replacing its original ledger primitives.

exploits.detail: The network halted 67 minutes when fragile quorum configuration lost sufficient overlap; safety held and no fork occurred.
A Protocol 23 archival bug corrupted 478 entries before detection; most were repaired, while 84 required protocol or issuer mitigation.

sanctions.detail: No chain-level designation is asserted; an archived exact-name SDN review remains an explicit gap.

risks.detail: SCP prioritizes safety over liveness; poor quorum selection or insufficient intersection can halt consensus.
The 2025 Soroban archival incident shows that new smart-contract storage machinery can corrupt application state without halting base payments.
Issued assets and offchain redemption depend on anchors or issuers even when settlement is on Stellar.

synthesis.situation: Stellar carries $937.8M stablecoin supply, $215.1M DeFi TVL, and $2.89M in 30-day fees, while Soroban expands programmability and recent archival bugs expose a newer state-risk surface.
synthesis.postmortem: The 2019 halt validated SCP's safety-over-liveness design; the 2025 archival event instead showed that ledger progress can continue while a storage feature corrupts limited application state.
synthesis.why: Stellar persists because payments, issuance, anchors, and institutional distribution were first-class before DeFi, while Soroban added programmability without discarding proven settlement rails.
synthesis.success_mechanism: Low-cost XLM-funded accounts and fees, native asset exchange, SCP finality, anchor integrations, and WASM contracts support payment and programmable-finance workflows.
strategic_choices: Use federated Byzantine agreement instead of proof of work or stake.
Prioritize payments and asset issuance before general smart contracts.
Add Soroban as a WASM contract system through a phased validator-approved rollout.
unknowns: Current Tier-1 quorum, infrastructure-provider, issuer, and stablecoin concentration.
How much SDF-held XLM will enter circulation and under what mandate schedule.
Whether post-incident archival verification catches future state corruption before application impact.
lessons_learned: Consensus safety, liveness, and application-state correctness are separate properties.
Payments-chain health is understated by DeFi TVL alone.
Phased feature rollout limits but does not eliminate novel storage risk.
synthesis.could_differ: Launching Turing-complete contracts earlier could have captured more DeFi, but would have increased attack and state-growth surface before the payment rail matured.

outlook.bull: Soroban converts institutional payment distribution into durable programmable finance.
outlook.base: Stellar remains a major payment and stablecoin rail with moderate DeFi growth.
outlook.bear: Quorum concentration, issuer dependence, or state bugs limit application trust.

live.title: Flare public token distribution and live launch

flr.title: Flare FLR supply and utility documentation

stables.title: DefiLlama stablecoin supply by chain API

lifecycle.description: Flare mainnet genesis began in observation mode with Foundation-operated validation and rollback risk.
Public FLR distribution began after the network passed its decentralization threshold.
The 36-month FlareDrop distribution concluded.
Governance accepted FIP.16 to reduce inflation and route ecosystem income toward supply reduction and growth.

token.launch_relation: FLR balances existed at genesis, but the public TDE followed decentralization in January 2023; the final scheduled FlareDrop ended in January 2026.

capital.notes: Primary sources name early backers and token allocations but do not reconcile cash proceeds across all rounds. Backer-token reinvestment commitments are not financing totals.

onchain.methodology_note: Metrics cover tracked chain activity, not offchain value referenced by Flare data protocols or all FAsset collateral.

team.entity: Flare Foundation supports protocol development and governance; Flare Labs builds ecosystem protocols, with validators and data providers participating in network operation.

key_events.description: The Foundation initially operated validation during observation mode.
Public distribution began after external validation passed the launch threshold.

narrative.purpose: Make external blockchain and internet data available natively to EVM contracts through network-secured oracles, data acquisition, and FAssets.
narrative.positioning: A data-centric EVM L1 combining FTSO price feeds, the Flare Data Connector, and cross-chain asset protocols.
narrative.narrative_arc: Flare moved from a long XRP-holder distribution to a data-protocol L1, completed token distribution, launched deeper asset protocols, and then reworked token economics to restore FLR value capture.

sanctions.detail: No chain-level designation is asserted; an archived exact-name SDN review remains an explicit gap.

risk.audit_status: Validator and FAssets reviews are public, including a 2026 OpenZeppelin trust-model audit; a complete current ecosystem audit inventory is not asserted.

risks.detail: FAssets and data applications depend on timely, manipulation-resistant FTSO and external-state acquisition.
The FAssets audit identifies exclusive governance control of foundational address-update mechanisms as a trust assumption.
FIP.16 explicitly responds to earlier design choices that reduced FLR's ecosystem role, proving value capture was not automatic.

synthesis.situation: Flare holds $113.4M TVL and $151.6M in 30-day DEX volume, while FLR is 95.8% below its launch-day high and governance is actively rebuilding token value capture.
synthesis.why: Flare remains relevant because it embeds oracle and external-state services into the L1 rather than requiring every application to assemble a separate data and bridge stack.
synthesis.success_mechanism: Validators, FTSO providers, and data-connector participants supply external data; FAssets and applications create demand; FIP.16 routes income toward ecosystem and supply reduction.
strategic_choices: Build an EVM L1 around native data protocols.
Delay public token distribution until validation decentralized beyond Foundation control.
Use governance to revise inflation and income routing when FLR value capture weakened.
unknowns: Current validator, FTSO-provider, FAsset-agent, collateral, and application-TVL concentration.
The realized cash financing and current Foundation treasury.
Whether FIP.16 income mechanisms produce material recurring FLR demand after implementation.
lessons_learned: Token distribution, network genesis, and decentralization thresholds are separate lifecycle events.
Native data reduces integration friction but concentrates oracle and governance risk in the base layer.
Protocol activity does not guarantee native-token value capture without explicit routing.
synthesis.could_differ: Keeping oracle services application-level would simplify base-layer trust, but sacrifice Flare's main distribution and composability advantage.

outlook.bull: FAssets and native data become widely used and FIP.16 creates sustainable FLR-linked income.
outlook.base: Flare keeps a meaningful data-and-DeFi niche with modest token capture.
outlook.bear: Oracle, collateral, or governance failures overwhelm usage and token reforms.

pivot.title: Cronos Labs vertically integrated product pivot

stables.title: DefiLlama stablecoin supply by chain API

lifecycle.description: Cronos EVM mainnet beta launched as a Cosmos-SDK EVM chain with CRO gas and IBC connectivity.
Crypto.org Coin and the ecosystem rebranded around Cronos and CRO.
Cronos zkEVM launched as a separate Ethereum L2 using zkCRO gas; it is not collapsed into this Cronos EVM dossier.
Cronos Labs announced a shift from generic L1 blockspace toward vertically integrated first-party financial applications and CRO buy-and-burn economics.

token.launch_relation: CRO predates Cronos EVM and serves multiple Crypto.com/Cronos networks; it pays Cronos EVM gas, while sibling Cronos zkEVM uses liquid-staked zkCRO.

capital.notes: Cronos Labs disclosed a $100M accelerator/ecosystem fund. That commitment is not counted as chain financing or current liquid treasury.

onchain.methodology_note: These metrics cover Cronos EVM only and must not be combined with Cronos POS or Cronos zkEVM.

team.entity: Cronos Labs develops and grows the Cronos ecosystem in partnership with Crypto.com distribution; independent validators operate the Cosmos-SDK network.

key_events.description: Particle B rebranded as Cronos Labs and continued the $100M ecosystem program.
Ryan Wyatt became Cronos Labs CEO and announced the vertically integrated product strategy.

narrative.purpose: Bring Crypto.com users into self-custodial EVM DeFi and gaming through a Cosmos-SDK chain, bridges, and first-party applications.
narrative.positioning: Cronos EVM is the Cosmos-SDK EVM L1 in a three-chain Cronos family alongside Cronos POS and Cronos zkEVM; strategy is shifting toward Crypto.com-distributed financial products.
narrative.narrative_arc: Cronos rapidly bootstrapped DeFi through Crypto.com and IBC, lost most peak TVL, expanded into a separate zkEVM, and then rebooted around owned apps and direct CRO value capture.

sanctions.detail: No chain-level designation is asserted; an archived exact-name SDN review remains an explicit gap.

risks.detail: Scheduled binary upgrades pause the chain until enough validators update, exposing liveness to coordinated operations.
Cronos relies on IBC and bridges for CRO and external assets, creating cross-chain implementation and liquidity risk.
Cronos EVM, POS, and zkEVM have distinct security, gas, and liquidity domains that branding can obscure.

synthesis.situation: Cronos EVM retains $255.3M TVL and $179.5M stablecoin supply but is 92.1% below its 2022 TVL peak, motivating a pivot from generic blockspace toward owned financial products.
synthesis.why: Cronos reached scale because Crypto.com distribution and CRO rails lowered onboarding friction, but undifferentiated EVM DeFi did not preserve peak liquidity.
synthesis.success_mechanism: Crypto.com can route users and assets into Cronos; IBC and EVM compatibility attract apps; first-party products may send fees toward CRO buy-and-burn.
strategic_choices: Build a Cosmos-SDK EVM chain with IBC and CRO gas.
Operate Cronos POS and zkEVM as distinct sibling networks rather than one chain.
Pivot toward vertically integrated, revenue-generating first-party applications.
unknowns: Current validator, application-TVL, bridge, and Crypto.com-routing concentration.
Current CRO supply, market metrics, treasury holdings, and exact buy-and-burn implementation.
Whether first-party applications rebuild durable TVL without crowding out independent builders.
lessons_learned: Exchange distribution accelerates launch but does not make generic blockspace defensible.
Sibling chains must be measured separately to avoid mixing gas, security, and activity.
A 92% TVL drawdown can coexist with a still-material ecosystem and motivate strategy change.
synthesis.could_differ: Staying a neutral general-purpose L1 might preserve builder neutrality, but would leave Cronos competing on increasingly commoditized EVM blockspace.

outlook.bull: First-party apps and Crypto.com distribution rebuild usage with explicit CRO value capture.
outlook.base: Cronos remains a material but below-peak exchange ecosystem while the pivot develops.
outlook.bear: Liquidity fragments across sibling chains and owned apps fail to reverse decline.
